## Languages

**Languages** (decided 19 October 2026, replacing the relay chain of 18 October). The game keeps one mediator between two kings, the envoy, because he is the one with a motive to bend a message, and because one mediator keeps the message trail readable: what the king wrote, what the envoy said abroad, what the host answered and what the envoy reported home ("The message trail"). His choice costs output only when he makes it: he passes his king's words on as written, or reports an answer as given, with a flag, the engine copies the text, and only what he changes or adds is written out ("Output is the other half"). A chain of scribes and interpreters, each rolling for loss and each deciding how faithful to be, was dropped: it added many steps that could go wrong, was hard to balance, cost several model calls a round trip, buried the envoy's choices in noise, and gave the extra mediators almost no reason to lie.

**Language skill buys time, never noise.** Like every other skill, a character's skill in each language is a hidden number from 0 to 100, never shown to players. When something has to cross a language, whoever does the crossing sets the chance that it succeeds this season, rolled each season until it does: from about 80 it succeeds at once; below that, the chance each season is roughly the skill as a percentage; at 0 it never does, until someone learns. Where two people are involved, the weaker skill counts. Nothing is garbled; a weak speaker is slow. In words, for a character's persona, its claims and the narrator, the number reads as none, halting, good or fluent: a model character knows its Hittite is "good", and may boast that it is fluent.

- **Speaking.** The envoy is understood when he and someone at the host's court, the king or any servant, share a language; the chance comes from the poorer of the two in their best shared language, any language counting, a court's or not. A servant who bridges passes the envoy's words on faithfully, since he has nothing to gain by changing them, unless he is in someone else's pay ("A go-between for hire"). The same rule holds between any two characters in the same place: each season they try, and once they understand each other the whole message passes, never garbled ("Characters deal with each other"; decided 21 October 2026). The dice fall first (decided 21 October 2026): at the start of each season, before any model is called, the engine settles who understands whom, for every pair of characters in the same place and every envoy at a court, and each character's request says whom he can make himself understood to this season. He writes only to them, so no call is spent on words nobody will understand, and one who badly wants to talk to someone waits and tries again next season. When nobody at a court understands an envoy, the king is told so plainly (below), and the envoy's model is never asked to speak.
- **A go-between for hire (decided 21 October 2026).** Two characters with no shared language can hire a third who speaks both to bridge for them, on a job like any other ("Jobs, not wages"), and a court can hire one for an envoy nobody there understands. He can also post a standing price where he lives, for each pair of languages he bridges, and anyone there may use him at that price without bargaining, paying him for each message he carries across; a script go-between sets his price by expected income, as for any fee ("Fees clear the market"). The dice that settle who understands whom count him in ("Speaking"), so a character's request lists whom he can reach through a go-between and at what price, and no call is spent on haggling. Each side is understood through him by the same chance, from the weakest skill along the way. So a man with several languages at a busy door, Ugarit or Alashiya's port where strangers land, can live on it ("Working for oneself"), as interpreters did: Akkadian already had a word for him, targumannu, the root of "dragoman". He follows the scribe's rule ("A king seals what his scribe wrote"), as a bridging court servant does. An ordinary go-between passes the words on faithfully, since he has no motive to do otherwise, and the engine relays them with no model call. One in someone else's pay, bribed by the other side or by a third party, may bend what he passes on, softening a threat, inflating an offer or dropping a condition; only then is his model called, once for each message he bridges, so honesty costs nothing and only a real betrayal costs a call. The pay is a fact the engine holds, a motive with a name on it: he is in someone else's pay when the engine holds a job, or gold handed to him, from anyone other than whoever pays him for this exchange (for a court servant, anyone other than his own king), given within the past year or still in force. Anyone present who understands both languages may notice the difference, by the same chance as in "Speaking", and it becomes something he knows and can sell or tell ("What servants know"); otherwise the victim learns only when the consequences come back. Either way the go-between hears every word, so, like the scribe, he can be bribed, questioned or spied on, and can sell what he heard.
- **An envoy not yet understood chooses** whether to stay until he is, go home, or lie and report that his message was delivered. Lying saves time, and his king may not learn the truth for a year; the choice has a motive, and it is his. While he stays, he learns.
- **Where nobody at court shares any language with him,** the king is told so plainly ("nobody at your court understands him; he presented gifts weighing 40 shekels"), never shown gibberish, which a model would try to decode. Gifts are then the only language until someone learns, and the easiest thing for an envoy to steal from.
- **Reading a tablet.** The king chooses who translates it, and the chance comes from the translator's weaker skill of the two languages concerned, the tablet's and the king's. An unreadable tablet waits until a reader is found (see "Tablets are objects in a place"); an urgent one is a reason to hire a better reader.
- **Composing.** A king speaks his own language, so his envoy must grasp it. A native servant does so at once; a foreign hire with halting Egyptian needs longer to take in his mandate and leaves later, unless someone at court bridges for him. A tablet in a foreign language needs a scribe who writes it, and a weaker scribe takes longer.
- **Learning by living there.** Each season a character lives in a province, his skill rises in the languages spoken there, and only in those ("Where each language is spoken"; decided 21 October 2026), quickly at first and slowly near the top. How fast depends on a hidden aptitude for languages, from 0 to 100 like every skill; on how widely each language is spoken there; and on the share of the season he spent in the province, the same accounting as the road check, so a resident learns a full season's worth and a traveller passing through almost none. Nobody learns from the company he keeps: standing next to a Hittite teaches nothing. Detained envoys come home speaking their hosts' tongue, and a king can send a young servant to Hattusa only to learn Hittite, a better bet if the servant is quick. Aptitude is hidden like every skill: a character may claim to learn quickly, and only time tells. It is more common among scribes and merchants, who live by words.
- **"Alien" courts.** Where no language overlaps, two courts talk through a proxy court that understands both, invest years in learning, or exchange only gifts.

**Who speaks what.** Characters start with the languages of where they come from: their home court's language fluently, and Akkadian at a skill that depends on their background, highest for scribes, merchants and former envoys. People from trading cities like Ugarit may speak several. Arrivals during play take their languages from their origin in the same way. For a stranger from beyond the map, his reason for coming sets how much he knows of a map language and his door sets which (decided 21 October 2026): a trader or a soldier for hire who has come this way before has some of the language spoken where his door opens, broken Akkadian at Ugarit, some Luwian on Arzawa's coast, some Akkadian on the eastern road and the Gulf; a wanderer, a refugee or a man from the tin lands has none; and a local coming home is fluent in his own ("Arrivals come through doors"). His own tongue still counts, since any language two characters share lets them talk ("Speaking"). Kings and rulers follow the same rules: a king speaks his own court's language and whatever the sources give him, learns by living somewhere like anyone, and otherwise talks through a go-between, as Tushratta dictated in Hurrian and sealed letters written in Akkadian. A servant who speaks Akkadian and a rare court language, such as Hittite, well is valuable. A character knows its own skills, in words, so it seeks work where they are worth most and prices itself accordingly; kings hear only its claims, and only results show whether "I speak Hittite well" was true (see "Kings never see skills").

**The court languages.** About five, not seven: Egyptian, Hittite, Hurrian (Mitanni), Luwian (Arzawa) and Akkadian, which Babylonia and Assyria speak natively in their own dialects. Alashiya's own language is unknown (undeciphered in reality), and its letters are in Akkadian. Babylonian and Assyrian envoys need no second language for diplomacy, which is Babylon's cultural prestige in mechanical form and belongs on the balance checklist. Arzawa is the period's example of a court outside the Akkadian world: its correspondence with Egypt in the archive (EA 31 and 32) is in Hittite, its reply asks Egypt to keep writing in Hittite, and these two tablets are what first showed, in 1902, that Hittite is an Indo-European language. Which courts read which languages is map data.

**Where each language is spoken (decided 21 October 2026).** Which languages are spoken in each province, and how widely, is map data from the history pass. Everywhere there is the people's own tongue: Canaanite in the Levantine cities, whose scribes glossed their Akkadian letters with words of their own speech; Ugaritic at Ugarit; a Nubian tongue in Nubia; Luwian in Arzawa's lands; Hurrian across Mitanni. A court adds its own language, and Akkadian where it keeps Akkadian scribes. So the people's tongues are languages like any other, not only the five court languages above: two Levantine characters understand each other in Canaanite, and a newcomer at Ugarit can pick up the street's Ugaritic before the scribes' Akkadian. A character learns only what is spoken where he lives ("Learning by living there"), and which languages a court reads in its tablets stays a separate fact ("Reading a tablet").

**Calibration.** In the period nearly every great court kept Akkadian scribes, so if Akkadian is common, languages will rarely block anything. The interesting cases come from making it scarcer at the edges, perhaps at Arzawa or Alashiya; that is tuned from games. Arrivals already lean that way, since the western sea brings Aegeans with no Akkadian to exactly those coasts ("Arrivals come through doors").

**A lingua franca by incentive, not by rule.** Nothing makes Akkadian the language of diplomacy. A court is understood only where it shares a language, so courts drift toward whatever tongue the most servants speak, and Akkadian, spoken most widely, is the obvious candidate. If another language spread instead, through hiring or arrivals, the drift would follow it.

**Language is also how one hears.** What a character picks up at a foreign court, its gossip, rumours and careless talk, depends on its information-gathering skill and on how well it speaks that court's own language. An envoy who speaks Hittite well at Hattusa overhears what one speaking only Akkadian never will, which gives every language a value beyond carrying letters.

**Retired with the chain:** the per-sentence rolls, marked gaps and marked ambiguity, the combined roll and its curve, interpreters' and scribes' decisions over what they relay, and the five-version message trail. The per-season chance replaces them in item 12: language then costs time, not words. The old script rule that drops a letter's last sentence when competence is below 35 is retired in item 12 too: whether a message is altered is the envoy's choice, never his skill's. One decision returns, and only with a motive: a bridger in someone else's pay may bend what he passes on, by the scribe's rule ("A go-between for hire"; decided 21 October 2026).
